name: Print on demand business
blurb: Upload your designs; a print partner makes and ships each item only after it sells
title: Print on Demand Business: How It Works, Margins and Risks
description: How a print on demand business works, what eats the margin, what you need to start, the copyright traps to avoid and how to test designs before paying for ads.
h1: How to start a print on demand business
answer: Print on demand means you create designs, list them on products such as T-shirts, mugs or posters, and a print partner makes and ships each item only after a customer orders it. You earn the gap between your price and the partner's base cost, minus platform fees and marketing. The catch is that margins are thin, millions of similar designs compete for attention, and using other people's characters, logos or slogans can get your shop closed.

sections.h: How print on demand makes money
body: You connect a print provider to your own store or to a marketplace, upload a design and set a retail price. When an order comes in, the provider charges you its base price plus shipping, prints the item and sends it to the customer. You keep the rest after marketplace fees and payment fees.

Some marketplaces work the other way round: they set the price and pay you a royalty per sale. Either way, income comes from many small sales of many designs, so the work is design volume, niche research and getting found.

ul: Original designs, made by you or by a designer under a licence that allows commercial use.
An account with a print provider and either your own store or a marketplace that accepts print-on-demand sellers.
Sample orders of your own products so you know the print and fabric quality.
Mockup photos and product descriptions that are honest about materials and sizing.
Local paperwork: rules differ by country. Usually business registration and tax registration once you trade regularly; check with your local tax authority.
Time to research niches and publish designs consistently.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: Designers, illustrators and people with a strong niche sense of humour
People who plan to copy trending designs
Someone who wants to sell without buying stock
Anyone expecting high profit per item
Patient people who can publish many designs and learn from data
Sellers who want full control over print quality and delivery time

ul: Copyright and trademark: designs using brands, sports teams, film characters, celebrity likenesses or trademarked phrases lead to takedowns and account bans. Search a phrase before using it.
Thin margins: base cost and shipping are fixed by the provider, so discounts and ads quickly eat the profit.
Quality and delays you do not control, which still show up in your reviews.
Saturation and design theft: popular designs get copied, and generic slogans compete with thousands of others.
Hype: courses promising automated stores or AI-generated design bundles rarely mention the IP and quality problems.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Choose a narrow audience you understand, such as a hobby, profession or local identity.
Make ten original designs for that audience.
Order one sample to check the print, colours and fit.
List the designs on one platform and share them where that audience gathers, within each community's rules.
Work out profit per item after base cost, shipping and fees, and see which designs get views and favourites.
Register the business if required and set up a separate account to track income and costs.
Pick one provider and one sales channel to keep things simple.
Publish a batch of original designs each week in your chosen niche.
Check every phrase and image for trademarks or copyrighted elements before listing.
Review which designs and products get views or sales, and make variations of those.

faq.q: Is print on demand worth it?
faq.a: It is a low-cost way to learn online selling and test designs, but profit per item is small. It tends to work for people with a clear niche and original designs, not for generic or copied slogans.

Platforms and laws treat AI images differently, and they can still copy protected characters or styles by accident. Check your platform's rules and review every design for brand names, logos and recognisable characters.

faq.q: Do I need my own website?
faq.a: No. Many sellers start on a marketplace that already has shoppers. Your own store gives more control, but you then have to bring all the traffic yourself.
